articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed wasn't supposed to be a politician. Now he's America's 1st Muslim senator
articles.summary: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in the race for a US Senate seat in Michigan, marking a victory for the former public health
articles.body: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in the race for a US Senate seat in Michigan, marking a victory for the former public health official who entered politics after training as a doctor.With his victory, El-Sayed has made history as the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.The closely fought contest marks a breakthrough for the party’s progressive faction and prevents Republicans from flipping the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.El-Sayed campaigned on an agenda centred on universal healthcare and government accountability in one of the country's key political battleground states.The Michigan race had drawn national attention as Democrats sought to regain control of the Senate.Rogers, a former congressman and chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, was making a second attempt to win a Senate seat after losing to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by fewer than 20,000 votes in 2024.For El-Sayed, the victory marks the culmination of a political journey that began with a career in medicine. According to his campaign website, he initially trained to become a doctor but came to believe that failures in the political system were contributing to people's health problems.He has since built his career around public health and government administration, including serving as director of the Wayne County Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services.His campaign focused on the idea that healthcare should be accessible to everyone and that government should work for ordinary Americans rather than wealthy individuals and corporations.'I believe life in America shouldn't be this hard'"I ran for the US Senate because I believe life in America shouldn't be this hard," El-Sayed said on his campaign website, adding that he would fight to build a government that worked for people rather than "Elon Musk, Donald Trump, or their billionaire friends".His campaign website also described him as someone who "wasn't supposed to be a politician".Vocal critic of IsraelThe Michigan contest was marked by disagreements over US support for Israel and accusations of antisemitism.El-Sayed, who has been a vocal critic of Israel, faced criticism over his response to a March attack on a Michigan synagogue. He later apologised to those who felt his comments were hurtful.Republicans also sought to link him to controversial political streamer Hasan Piker, with whom he had appeared during the Democratic primary.President Donald Trump repeatedly referred to El-Sayed as a "jihadist", although Republicans produced no evidence linking him to terrorist organisations.From medical school to the US SenateBorn and raised in southeast Michigan, El-Sayed attended public schools and captained his high school football, wrestling and lacrosse teams.He graduated from the University of Michigan with the highest distinction and played for its men's lacrosse team. He later earned a medical degree from Columbia University through a National Institutes of Health-funded fellowship and completed a second doctorate at the University of Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar.His father, Mohamed, is an Egyptian immigrant, while his stepmother, Jackie, belongs to a family that has lived in Michigan's Gratiot County since the 1800s.El-Sayed lives in Ann Arbor with Sarah and their two daughters, Emmalee and Serene.A second consecutive defeatRogers, 63, a former congressman and FBI agent, entered the contest with the backing of Trump and national Republicans. He sought to portray El-Sayed as a radical candidate sympathetic to Islamic extremism, citing alleged links to the Muslim Brotherhood, Reuters reported.The defeat marks Rogers' second consecutive loss in a Michigan Senate race. He narrowly lost the 2024 contest to Democrat Elissa Slotkin, even as Trump carried the state in that year's presidential election.El-Sayed's victory gives Democrats a win in a state that has not elected a Republican to the US Senate since 1994.The Karnataka connectionEl-Sayed's victory also has a personal connection to coastal Karnataka through his wife, Dr Sarah Jukaku, a psychiatrist whose family traces its roots to Bhatkal, around 140km from Mangaluru.Sarah is the granddaughter of Jukaku Shamshuddin, who served as deputy minister for finance in Mysore State under then chief minister BD Jatti.A Rhodes Scholar, El-Sayed met Sarah while they were students at the University of Michigan. He has spoken about his connection with her South Indian family and culture."Listen, I've been married in a South Indian family for 20 years, like. I'm well inducted now. You know, I might be more Indian than I'm Arab," he said in an interview.While the family has its roots in Bhatkal, most of its members are now settled in Bengaluru. Sarah's immediate family, meanwhile, has largely remained in the US.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: UK man jailed for 4 years after inventing 716 donors and filing 60 fake Gift Aid claims to fraudulently obtain £708,750, using the money to pay off mortgages and family debts
articles.summary: A UK man has been jailed for four years and eight months after inventing hundreds of charitable donations to fraudulently claim £708,750 from the
articles.body: A UK man has been jailed for four years and eight months after inventing hundreds of charitable donations to fraudulently claim £708,750 from the government through the Gift Aid scheme. Abdul Muttakin Robbani, 54, from Chelmsford, submitted 60 false claims through his organisation, RMI Club, naming 716 people as donors despite them never having made the contributions. According to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), many of those named had only completed online surveys for small payments and did not know the organisation. Robbani used the proceeds to pay off mortgages and personal and family debts.How did Robbani use fake donors to claim £708,750 from the governmentAccording to the CPS, Robbani's false claims identified 716 individuals as donors who had supposedly contributed between £5,000 and £10,000 each to RMI Club. However, the people whose names appeared on the claims had not made any such donations. Many of them had simply completed an online survey in return for a small payment and did not know RMI Club.Robbani told HMRC that the individuals had been recruited through a marketing survey called the 'Sigma Social Impact Programme'. The programme was linked to a cryptocurrency mining scheme called 'XO', which he had created. The claims presented the survey participants as people who had made substantial charitable contributions, although they had not donated the amounts recorded in the submissions.Why did HMRC investigate bank accounts with balances of just £1To make the fraudulent donations appear legitimate, Robbani moved money between bank accounts under his control, using the names of the supposed donors as payment references. The transactions were designed to create the impression that RMI Club had received large donations from multiple individuals.HMRC's banking analysis found that several of the accounts involved had balances of just £1 before the fraud took place. Investigators also examined the cryptocurrency scheme associated with the claims. A cryptocurrency expert commissioned during the investigation concluded that Robbani's XO token had no objective value.How did HMRC uncover Robbani's £708,750 fraudulent donation claimsThe investigation began in June 2021 when HMRC's compliance team identified concerns about the claims. The matter was subsequently referred to HMRC's Fraud Investigation Service, which interviewed a sample of the people named as donors and obtained banking records to establish how the money had moved.HMRC also secured an account freezing order and recovered £215,000 through forfeiture. A further £485,750 was traced to Robbani's personal bank account. The CPS confirmed that confiscation proceedings under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 are ongoing to recover the proceeds of the criminal activity.What did the CPS reveal about Robbani's use of public moneyThe money obtained through the scheme was used to settle significant personal and family debts. Robbani used the proceeds to pay off mortgages on two properties in Chelmsford and Ipswich. Both properties were subsequently transferred into his wife's name.Emma Beazley, a specialist prosecutor at the CPS's Serious Economic Organised Crime and International Directorate, said: "Gift Aid exists to boost the vital work of charities and sports clubs - Robbani cynically exploited that system for personal gain, pocketing hundreds of thousands of pounds of public money that should never have been his."She added that Robbani had gone to considerable lengths to conceal the fraud by falsely listing hundreds of innocent people as donors and creating a series of circular bank transactions to disguise his actions.What penalties did Robbani face for his £708,750 Gift Aid fraudAlongside his four-year-and-eight-month prison sentence, Robbani was disqualified from acting as a company director for 15 years. The court also imposed a Serious Crime Prevention Order lasting five years, which will begin after his release from prison.The CPS said that Robbani had previous convictions for deception and forgery dating back to the 1990s. In 2011, the Charity Commission also removed a charity chaired by him from its register following serious governance failures.Steve Doyle, Assistant Director at HMRC's Fraud Investigation Service, said: "Robbani stole money that was meant to support genuine charities and instead used it to pay off mortgages and debts."He added that tax fraud has consequences for public services and encouraged anyone with information about tax fraud or money laundering to report it through GOV.UK.Gift Aid is a government scheme that allows eligible charities and Community Amateur Sports Clubs to reclaim tax on donations made by UK taxpayers. The scheme increases the value of eligible donations by 25%. In Robbani's case, the CPS said the system was exploited through fabricated donor details and misleading financial transactions, resulting in hundreds of thousands of pounds being paid out from public funds.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fears for ancient woodlands as pressure grows to build more homes
articles.summary: Dozens of individual sites feature planned developments immediately next to woods, the BBC finds.
articles.body:
Ancient woodland campaigners fear a drive to build more houses could put some of England's oldest habitats under increasing pressure, despite government protections designed to prevent their loss.

The protected areas can only be built on or near in "wholly exceptional circumstances", according to planning policy.

But the Labour government's pledge to build 1.5 million new homes by the end of 2029 and the recent creation of the "grey belt" - areas of poorer quality open spaces that can be built on - are leaving ancient woodlands at threat, campaigners say.

A spokesman for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said ancient woodlands continued to benefit from "very clear and strong protections".

But the BBC has found dozens of individual sites which feature planned developments immediately next to the woods.

Among them are approved plans for 450 homes within yards of Hook Wood in Gillingham, Kent, which residents fear will have a devastating impact on local wildlife.

"We are already seeing cases where the existing protections are struggling," said Ancient Woodland UK chairwoman Lucy Grabe-Watson.

"We have seen a rise in concerns and alerts from local groups since recent planning reforms."

An ancient woodland is classed as existing continuously since at least the year 1600. The sites, described as "irreplaceable by Grabe-Watson, are considered some of the UK's richest habitats for wildlife.

The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) guidelines for local councils deciding planning applications in England say woods can be built on in "wholly exceptional circumstances", such as major infrastructure projects like HS2.

But Grabe-Watson said the grey belt policy made it more likely areas directly next to ancient woodland - previously protected under green belt laws - could be developed.

In the East Midlands, the growing demand for housing is raising concerns about development proposals on land bordering Chaddesden Wood Nature Reserve in Derby.

Helen Cherry, who has lived nearby for 40 years, is among more than 1,500 people objecting to plans for about 150 houses there.

"The wood is at least 400 years old, with mature hazel and oak trees," said the former cafe owner, who regularly walks her dog there.

She said building to the edge of the ancient woodland would leave the site "closed on all sides", making a "mockery" of the nature reserve and undermining its protected status.

"Many a day I've been brought to tears, stopped and looked across the field where the buildings may occur and you can see right out across to the Derbyshire Dales," she added.

"It's absolutely beautiful. If houses went ahead, the view would be completely obliterated - it would be very sad."

Derby City Council refused the plans in 2025, but surveyors were seen at the site over the summer. People living near the site said they feared developers JGP Properties Limited would come back with amended proposals.

JGP Properties told the Local Democracy Reporting Service its assessments demonstrated "no loss or deterioration of the ancient woodland and veteran trees".

The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds said protections for irreplaceable habitats had improved under the recent changes to the NPPF.

However, Carl Bunnage, head of nature policy for the charity, said they remained inadequate.

He argued allowing development in "wholly exceptional circumstances" represented a loophole for developers, especially in areas with a shortage of houses.

He said planning reforms were in favour of development, with housing and economic growth policies often carrying greater weight than nature conservation.

"If we can give the strongest protections to built heritage features such as historic buildings, then why shouldn't we also be giving the strongest protections to those habitats?" Bunnage said.

In South Yorkshire, concerns are being raised over the impact of a 130-home development on land surrounding Gelster Wood.

It has sparked a campaign in the village of Rossington, near Doncaster, with residents worried the proposal could permanently alter a centuries-old landscape.

More than 2,000 people have backed efforts to challenge the plans.

"People feel our village is being treated as an easy target for developers who don't care about our community or our heritage," said Gary Cantrill, a local beekeeper and member of the Preserve Littleworth Lane Group.

"This isn't just an empty plot. It's 350-year-old historic farmland."

He said residents were also worried about flooding as the fields currently absorbed "vast amounts of rainwater".

"Concreting over this land replaces natural drainage and creates a huge risk of flooding into neighbouring properties and roads," he added.

Matt Shardlow, an ecological consultant working with the campaign, said damage could be caused to ancient woodlands, even when trees were not removed.

Roots extending away from the sites could be damaged by development, he said, while drainage for nearby new housing could dry out certain tree species and pollute their water supplies.

Noise and light pollution could also drive sensitive species out of the woods, Shardlow added. Even having pet cats in an area could affect populations of ground-nesting birds, bats and other species, he said.

A spokesperson for developers Albemarle Homes said the woodland itself was not included in the original site and any future plans would have to comply with environmental rules.

A spokesman for the government's housing department said national planning rules "explicitly" stated developments that would cause the loss or deterioration of ancient woodland should be refused.

He added there were "very limited exceptions" to the policy, limited to some nationally significant infrastructure projects. He added in those cases compensation measures would be required.

The department said a revised NPPF published in August contained clearer policies for assessing development proposals affecting irreplaceable habitats.

articles.title: Defence production at Rs 1.78 lakh crore: Rajnath Singh sets out India's next priorities
articles.summary: Ongoing conflicts in west Asia and Ukraine have once again put a spotlight on the importance of indigenous weapons development and manufacturing.
articles.body: Ongoing conflicts in west Asia and Ukraine have once again put a spotlight on the importance of indigenous weapons development and manufacturing. As these two prolonged conflicts have shown that owning the most advanced weapons is no longer enough. Relatively inexpensive drones and autonomous systems are challenging sophisticated and costly platforms and battlefields now stretch beyond land, sea and air into space, cyberspace and the digital domain.While addressing the third edition of the Delhi Defence Dialogue at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (MP-IDSA), Defence Minister Rajnath Singh stated that military preparedness in the 21st century cannot be separated from technological and industrial preparedness. The two-day dialogue, brings together policymakers, military officials, industry representatives, academics and strategic experts.Beyond making in IndiaSingh said Aatmanirbharta should be understood as a quest for technological sovereignty. It does not mean producing everything at home, he said, but making sure critical defence requirements are not "held hostage to external dependencies". True self-reliance, in his words, means having the knowledge to design a platform, the technology to build it, the intellectual property to upgrade it and the ability to sustain it through its lifecycle. He added that this is not a retreat from the world but a sign of a more self-assured India that can engage international partners.The defence minister described reforms, Aatmanirbharta, international collaboration and exports as four pillars that must move together. Reforms show the willingness to change, self-reliance the determination to create, collaboration the confidence to partner and exports the readiness to compete. Without the other three, he said, self-reliance alone would limit India's technological horizons, industrial scale and global competitiveness, a point he tied to the ambition of becoming a developed nation by 2047.The numbers behind the pushDefence production reached a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, Singh said, while exports rose to Rs 38,424 crore, with Indian products now reaching more than 80 countries. The government has set targets of Rs 3 lakh crore in production and Rs 50,000 crore in exports by 2029. That would mean production nearly 70% above the current level and exports about 30% higher, which is why he called for improvements in manufacturing capacity, product quality and global competitiveness.He said the government wants more private participation in advanced programmes such as the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft, propulsion systems, the Advanced Towed Artillery Gun System, artillery ammunition and shipbuilding, with room for MSMEs, start-ups and academia. On foreign partnerships, he called for a shift from procurement and licensed manufacturing to co-development, co-production and shared innovation, with meaningful Indian participation in design, access to critical technologies, appropriate sharing of intellectual property and a place in global supply chains. India's large domestic market and pool of engineering talent, he said, offer foreign firms real opportunities.Research and the armed forcesSingh also said the armed forces must remain stakeholders in research and development, since their operational experience helps set priorities and judge which emerging technologies matter. At the same time, he said, scientists need the freedom to pursue unconventional ideas beyond immediate operational requirements. Innovations, he added, must move out of laboratories and prototype stages into production and induction.Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, speaking earlier on Aatmanirbharta in naval systems at 2047, called it a strategic necessity. He said India needs a navy that can fight, sustain and adapt without being constrained by external dependencies, and that self-reliance does not mean isolation. India, he said, should collaborate with friendly countries from a position of strength.Taken together, the two speeches point to the same lesson. With wars increasingly decided by who can innovate, manufacture and replenish fastest, the test for India's defence industry will be how well it turns record production into sustained capability.

articles.title: From education to housing protests, Palestine’s flag spreads across Europe
articles.summary: Symbols such as the flag and keffiyeh represent anti-colonial struggles but some question their use amid mass rallies.
articles.body:
The Palestinian flag and traditional keffiyeh scarf have been regular appearances at recent demonstrations across Europe over housing, education and the cost of living.

Palestinian symbols were also displayed in Northern Ireland, where a decades-old standoff risked reigniting historic grievances.

Kenny Pierre Agboton, from the Free University of Brussels for Palestine platform, says the use of the Palestinian flag in demonstrations is a nod to anti-colonialism and anti-repression struggles.

“From climate change to liveable Earth, the Palestinian issue becomes the crossroad for every fight we have, at least in Western Europe,” he told Al Jazeera.

He said that engaging in a political struggle is a political choice that values education over “giving arms to the military”.

His association is in contact with like-minded groups at other universities in Belgium and “we usually give one flag to each association” during nationwide demonstrations.

Across the border, France is witnessing nationwide rallies that began over faults within the education system.

High school students, backed by university and teacher associations, trade unions and some politicians, are demanding more affordable, higher-quality education, upgraded schools, smaller classes and more teachers. And some have done so while carrying the Palestinian flag or wearing the keffiyeh.

‘Global system organising attacks on our rights’

Alice Cohen-Morzadec, spokesperson for the French Student Union and a regular protester, views the flag as a symbol of the daily struggles in the occupied West Bank and Gaza and broader global inequalities.

“As young people, high school or university students, we know that these demonstrations are not just about our own situation; it is about a global system that is organising attacks on our rights,” she said. “It is a broader movement against world capitalism and colonialism system.”

Some politicians support using the symbols, too.

Nelson Mandela wore the keffiyeh in 1990. In 2006, then-Spanish Prime Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero of the Socialist Workers’ Party briefly wore one after a young Palestinian reportedly placed it around his neck.

“What’s wrong with a citizen taking to the streets with a Palestinian flag?” said Mario Furore, an Italian member of the European Parliament from the Five Star Movement, which belongs to The Left parliamentary group. “Should we really be outraged by this, when the Israeli government is accused of genocide in Gaza and continues to massacre Palestinians in the West Bank? We mustn’t make the mistake of relativising everything,” he said.

“Since October 7, 2023, Israeli operations have caused tens of thousands of Palestinian deaths, nearly 80,000 according to some estimates. This fact alone should put things into perspective.”

But the anti-colonial messaging of the students or the realpolitik of some politicians does not resonate in every country with a protest movement.

Fatos Lubonja, an activist and writer who spent 17 years in prison during Albania’s communist rule, said he is one of the few who has carried the Palestinian flag or worn a keffiyeh during anticorruption demonstrations in his Muslim-majority country over the past four months.

He said that in Albania , some see the Palestinian struggle alongside issues related to Muslims. And Muslims are equated with the Ottoman Empire.

“We were liberated from the Ottomans. The Ottomans were considered as occupiers with whom we lived with a long time. The narrative was that we were coming back to Europe, returning to our roots,” he said.

“Being a Muslim for Albanians during communism means you had to be emancipated, that we wanted to be [a] Westerner, part of NATO. That is why Albanians, even today, are very pro-American and, of course, being pro-American means you also have to be pro-Israel,” he said.

Seeing the Palestinian cause and flag waved at European demonstrations is not to everyone’s liking, especially since some violent protesters have also brandished Palestinian symbols.

Palestinian writer and researcher Waddah Abu Jamea, writing in Al Majalla magazine in October, described discomfort watching on.

“Palestinians consequently find themselves expected to condemn the thief while thanking the student or academic who raises their flag. They watch as the flag’s original meaning disappears behind a cacophony of competing causes and agendas. They see it enlisted in struggles over identity, immigration, religion and security. At the same time, their own story, like the Palestinians’ collective national cause, fades into the background amid the growing politicisation of solidarity,” he wrote.

“The flag has crossed borders, but those borders remain closed off to Palestinians. It has entered universities and institutions while schools in Gaza have been destroyed, depriving Palestinian children of access to education. It flies above demonstrations in Paris, while Palestinians in the West Bank are denied the freedom to carry it in protest against killing, imprisonment, and siege.”

Some sent blunter messages to the student protesters.

Janine di Giovanni, a journalist and the head of The Reckoning Project, which documents war crimes, was visiting the West Bank on October 18 when she posted about the French protesters on her Facebook page.

She said that as she lives in Paris and has worked in Palestine for more than 30 years, she understands the root of the European protests.

“But I am writing this from the West Bank, where I document what is happening to Palestinian families during the olive harvest,” she wrote. “Every day there is violence. … So I ask you, gently: please don’t link your struggle to Palestine.”

“Not because yours doesn’t matter, but because they are not the same. Palestinians are fighting for something more basic: the right to live freely and safely on their own land. When the two are conflated, it blurs what is happening here and gives those who already misunderstand both causes an easy excuse to dismiss them, or to see only violence. Fight for your future. It is worth fighting for. But let Palestine’s story be told on its own terms.”

articles.title: Guernsey’s 18th-century windmill became a German observation tower during World War II; it is now on sale for £2.95 million with planning permission for a six-floor home
articles.summary: Vale Mill in Guernsey, a historic windmill that later served as a Second World War German lookout tower, has been listed for sale at a guide price of
articles.body: Vale Mill in Guernsey, a historic windmill that later served as a Second World War German lookout tower, has been listed for sale at a guide price of £2.95 million. Standing 69 feet (21 metres) tall in the parish of Vale and now renamed The Lookout, the granite building is visible across the island. Planning permission has already been secured to convert it into a striking modern home, making it a rare redevelopment opportunity. The tower stands beside a water-filled quarry, and the sale offers a piece of island heritage and an approved blueprint to bring it back to life.How a wooden windmill built in 1770 became a granite landmark and a wartime lookout postSavills Guernsey said the original structure was built from wood in 1770 before being rebuilt in granite in 1854. It worked as a flour windmill until the German occupation of 1940, when it was turned into an observation tower. The States of Guernsey, the island’s government, was gifted the building in 1968. It sold the mill into private ownership 40 years later, after the structure had fallen into disrepair.Inside the approved plans, four bedrooms, an underground extension and a floating summer houseThe planning consent, granted in 2020 for the protected building, covers a six-floor, four-bedroom home with a kitchen and dining area, a utility room and a breakfast room. It also includes an observation deck, a terrace, garaging and a substantial basement extension that cantilevers out over the quarry.That extension would be built within the quarry’s rock face and designed to blend with the mill, with large windows opening onto a balcony deck. An underground link beneath the driveway would join it to the tower. A walkway would lead from the main house towards a floating summer house. The top two former German observation levels could become offices or entertaining spaces.The open market rule that lets British passport holders purchase the millThe property is available through Guernsey’s open market, so it can be bought by anyone with a British passport or the right to reside in the United Kingdom. It is the first property to qualify under a new rule for exceptional circumstances, introduced in 2025. The island’s Committee for Housing gave it an open market listing in principle because of its cultural importance. The tower will be fully inscribed on the open market register only once the development is completed in line with the approved planning permissions. Local market homes make up most of Guernsey’s housing and are reserved for people with a local licence or the right to work on the island.Deputy Sasha Kazantseva-Miller, vice president of the Committee for Housing, told the BBC that members wanted to encourage new homes while preserving buildings that form part of the island’s historic and cultural heritage. She added that the in-principle approval should help bring in the significant investment a property of this nature requires.Nick Paluch, a director in the residential sales team at Savills Guernsey, said the sale represents a rare opportunity. He described the mill as a landmark that offers the kind of diversity the island needs to keep attracting new investment, and as a chance for a buyer to create a top-quality home in the spirit of the television series Grand Designs.Restoration work completed so far and views the mill’s owners say are the best on the islandJames Ridout, director of Vale Mill Limited, said his father bought the building at auction in 2008 with a business partner. Ridout has since restored the tower to prepare the site for further development. The work has included repointing the stonework, making the structure wind and watertight, adding staircases, and clearing and landscaping the land around the quarry.Ridout also told the BBC that without the listing, further investment was unviable and the building risked falling into disrepair again and possibly being “permanently lost”. He described the views from the top of the tower as “the best in Guernsey”, with the sea visible for miles around.Demand for Guernsey property remains strong, with buyers drawn to the lifestyle and business linksPaluch said Guernsey continues to attract would-be buyers and that activity has been strong since the start of 2026. He pointed to the island’s scenery and outdoor lifestyle, its growing reputation as a centre of excellence for business and finance, and its strong community. He also cited good schools, low crime rates and a favourable tax regime.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: James Bond star Daniel Craig calls inheritance 'distasteful', doesn't want his daughters inheriting his millions and plans to give away his fortune; has donated $90,000 worth of motorcycles to charity
articles.summary: James Bond actor Daniel Craig has a rather unusual philosophy about wealth and inheritance.
articles.body: James Bond actor Daniel Craig has a rather unusual philosophy about wealth and inheritance. The actor, who earned millions playing the iconic British secret agent, has said he does not want his daughters to inherit a large fortune, describing the very idea of passing down substantial wealth as "distasteful". Instead, Craig believes people should use their money or give it away during their lifetimes rather than leave enormous sums behind. His views are reflected in some of his charitable activities, including donating two limited-edition motorcycles associated with his Bond films to raise funds for the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI). He has also supported United Nations efforts to clear landmines and explosive hazards around the world.Why Daniel Craig consider inheritance 'distasteful'Craig first spoke about his inheritance philosophy in a 2020 interview with Saga Magazine, saying he did not want to leave large sums of money to the next generation. He repeated the position in an August 2021 interview with Candis Magazine, explaining that he preferred to give away his wealth before his death.The actor also referred to Scottish-American industrialist and philanthropist Andrew Carnegie, who gave away a substantial portion of his fortune to charitable causes. Craig estimated that Carnegie's donations would amount to around $11 billion in today's money."Isn't there an old adage that if you die a rich person, you've failed?" Craig said, before adding that he did not want to leave great sums to the next generation."My philosophy is: get rid of it or give it away before you go," he added.Daniel Craig donates two James Bond motorcycles to charityIn October 2024, Craig donated two limited-edition Triumph motorcycles from his personal collection to raise money for the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), a charity providing lifeboat and lifeguard rescue services across the UK and Ireland.The motorcycles, a Scrambler 1200 Bond Edition and a Tiger 900 Bond Edition, were inspired by the bikes featured in his final James Bond film, No Time to Die. Both were signed by the actor and auctioned through Bonhams.The Scrambler sold for £28,000, while the Tiger fetched £32,000, taking the total raised to £60,000. The entire amount went to the RNLI to support its lifesaving work during its 200th anniversary year.Craig has maintained a long association with the organisation, having grown up near its lifeboat station in Hoylake, England. He has also previously visited lifeboat crews to experience their rescue operations firsthand.How Daniel Craig helped raise more than $1 million for UN mine-clearance workCraig's charitable work has also extended to humanitarian efforts in countries affected by landmines and unexploded weapons. In 2015, then-UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon appointed him the organisation's first Global Advocate for the Elimination of Mines and Explosive Hazards.In the role, Craig helped draw international attention to the dangers posed by landmines and supported fundraising for the United Nations Trust Fund for Assistance in Mine Action. According to the UN, he helped raise more than $1 million for mine-action programmes during his tenure.One major fundraising initiative in 2019, organised with the United Nations Foundation and fundraising platform Omaze, generated $1.2 million. The money supported programmes in mine-affected countries, including Cambodia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mali and Nigeria.Craig also championed the UN's Safe Ground campaign, which promotes converting land cleared of mines into places for community activities, sports and recreation. His eight-year tenure as Global Advocate concluded in April 2023.Who are Daniel Craig's daughters?Craig has two daughters from his marriages. His elder daughter, Ella, was born in November 1992 during his marriage to Scottish actress Fiona Loudon. The couple married in 1992 and divorced in 1994.His younger daughter was born in September 2018 to Craig and his wife, actor Rachel Weisz, whom he married in 2011. The couple have largely kept their daughter's identity and family life private.Craig is also stepfather to Henry, Weisz's son from her previous relationship with filmmaker Darren Aronofsky.You use AI every day. articles.title: Blue trumps Red: 10 key takeaways from US midterm elections
articles.summary: The 2026 US midterm elections have delivered a political earthquake in Washington.
articles.body: The 2026 US midterm elections have delivered a political earthquake in Washington. Two years after Donald Trump returned to the White House promising to reshape American politics, voters have handed his Republican Party a stunning electoral rebuke, with Democrats capturing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.What was expected to be a difficult midterm test for the party in power has turned into a sweeping Democratic resurgence. Republicans have lost traditionally safe seats, several Trump-backed candidates have been defeated, and Democrats have made significant gains in states that the president carried comfortably in the 2024 presidential election.The results represent more than a change in congressional arithmetic. They raise serious questions about Trump's political standing, the durability of the MAGA movement, the future of Republican leadership and the balance of power in Washington ahead of the 2028 presidential election.The election also produced a string of landmark victories, including gains for Indian-American candidates, historic breakthroughs for minority candidates and major gubernatorial upsets.Here are the 10 biggest takeaways from the 2026 US midterm election results.1. Democrats capture Congress The biggest story of the election is the Democrats' return to power in both chambers of Congress, reversing the Republican dominance that followed Trump's 2024 victory.In the 100-member Senate, Democrats have secured at least seven Republican-held seats, taking their projected strength to 54 seats against 44 for Republicans, with two races still uncalled in the latest available tally. The Democratic total includes two independents who caucus with the party.The Senate breakthrough is particularly significant because Republicans entered the election with control of the chamber and Democrats needed to overcome a difficult map to reclaim the majority.In the 435-member House of Representatives, Democrats have crossed the crucial 218-seat threshold needed for control. More than two dozen Republican-held districts have been flipped, including constituencies that backed Trump by double-digit margins in 2024.The scale of the reversal is striking. The party that controlled the White House and both chambers after the previous election now faces a Congress dominated by its political opponents.Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become Speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January 2027. If elected, he would become the first Black politician to hold the powerful position.The implications are immediate: Democrats will be able to block legislation, scrutinise government spending, reject presidential nominees and launch congressional investigations into the Trump administration.2. Blue wave breaks Red wallPerhaps the most consequential aspect of the results is not simply the number of seats Democrats have won, but where they have won them.Read also | US midterms: Democrats flip over 35 Congressional seat, 4 governorshipsThe party has broken through in states and congressional districts that were considered reliably Republican, suggesting that the backlash against Trump extended well beyond traditional Democratic strongholds.The Senate provided some of the clearest evidence of this shift.Democrats flipped at least seven Republican-held seats:Texas: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, delivering one of the most consequential upsets of the election.Kansas: Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Republican Roger Marshall, ending a 94-year stretch without a Democratic senator from the state.Iowa: Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson.Ohio: Former governor Sherrod Brown defeated Republican incumbent Jon Husted.Maine: Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican senator Susan Collins.North Carolina: Democrat Roy Cooper defeated Republican Michael Whatley.South Carolina: Annie Andrews handed the Democrats a major win after defeating Darlene Graham.These victories are especially important because several of these states had backed Trump comfortably in 2024.The House results reinforced the trend.Democrats flipped over 30 Republican-held districts, including Indiana's 5th Congressional District, where Democrat JD Ford defeated incumbent Victoria Spartz in a constituency Trump had carried by nearly 17 percentage points.In Iowa, Democrats captured three of the state's four congressional districts, despite Republicans having held all four before the election.3. Referendum on Trump Trump repeatedly made himself the centre of the Republican campaign, urging supporters to treat the midterms as a verdict on his presidency.He repeatedly told voters to "pretend" he's on the ballot the past few months. “When Trump's on the ballot," he told Fox News in August, "they win".That strategy backfired spectacularly as voters took his advice.The president spent much of his second term pushing an expansive agenda covering immigration, tariffs, federal government restructuring, foreign policy and executive authority.The election gave voters an opportunity to register their disapproval of that agenda.Trump's difficulties are particularly evident in states that he won in 2024 but where Republican candidates have now been defeated.Democrats have made historic gains in Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and other traditionally conservative territory.The president, however, sought to distance himself from the losses. In comments following the results, he congratulated Democrats for campaigning effectively but argued that the election was not a personal setback."I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," he declared on Truth Social.Later he told news channels that he did not view the verdict as a "hit" on him, while blaming some Republican candidates for their defeats.But the political reality is that Trump had actively associated himself with the Republican candidates and their campaigns. Their defeats therefore raise questions about whether his endorsement still carries the electoral influence it once did.4. Economy tanked Trump The economy has once again proved to be one of the most powerful forces shaping American electoral behaviour.While Trump campaigned on promises to bring down prices, revive American industry and make life more affordable, voters have continued to grapple with the cost of everyday essentials.Inflation, fuel prices, household expenses and the broader cost of living emerged as important concerns in the election.The economic pressure was particularly visible in rural and midwestern communities, where residents often depend on cars for long-distance travel to workplaces, schools, hospitals and shopping centres. Higher petrol and diesel prices therefore had a direct impact on household budgets.The war involving the US, Israel and Iran has added another dimension to the economic problem. Disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting pressure on energy markets have contributed to higher fuel costs, making an already difficult affordability debate more politically damaging.Trump's tariff policies have also become a source of concern. Although the administration presented tariffs as a way to protect American manufacturing and strengthen domestic industries, businesses and consumers have faced the possibility of higher costs on imported goods.The Democratic campaign successfully connected these economic pressures to the administration's decisions.According to the AP Voter Poll, voters were concerned about high costs and wanted Congress to exercise greater oversight of the president. The economic message appears to have resonated even in constituencies that had previously supported Trump.5. Iran war hurts TrumpOne of the biggest political complications for Trump has been the war involving Iran, which has exposed a widening gap between his foreign policy decisions and the expectations of sections of his own voter base.Trump had returned to office promising to avoid prolonged foreign military engagements and prioritise American interests at home. His decision to enter the conflict alongside Israel has complicated that promise.The war has had consequences beyond the battlefield. Rising energy prices, uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz and concerns about the economic fallout have brought the conflict directly into the lives of ordinary Americans.The issue has also divided Trump's political coalition. While some Republican voters have supported a more aggressive foreign policy, others have questioned why the administration became involved in another major overseas conflict.Early CBS News exit polling found that most voters believed the US had made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran. Opposition extended beyond Democratic voters, with roughly a quarter of Republicans also expressing disapproval.The AP Voter Poll, which surveyed approximately 80,000 voters, found that the economy and the state of American democracy were the leading concerns. The Iran war added to the dissatisfaction surrounding the administration.6. Young & Hispanic voters ditch TrumpThe 2024 presidential election had demonstrated Trump's ability to attract voters beyond the traditional Republican base. His improved performance among Hispanic voters, younger men and sections of working-class America had helped him secure a decisive return to the White House.The 2026 midterms, however, suggest that this coalition is showing signs of fragmentation.The AP Voter Poll, based on approximately 80,000 voters across all 50 states, provides some of the clearest evidence of the shift.Among voters under 30, approximately seven in 10 backed Democratic candidates in their local House races, compared with three in 10 supporting Republicans. This represents a substantial change from 2024, when younger voters were roughly evenly divided between Trump and Kamala Harris.Hispanic voters also appeared to move away from the Republican Party. Approximately six in 10 Hispanic voters supported Democratic House candidates, while four in 10 backed Republicans.The shift was particularly visible along the Texas-Mexico border, where Democrats registered significant victories. Latin Grammy-winning candidate Bobby Pulido defeated Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz, reflecting the party's improved performance among Hispanic voters in the region.The Democratic gains among these groups are significant because Trump's 2024 victory had partly depended on expanding the Republican coalition among voters who had traditionally leaned Democratic.7. Democrats flip governorshipsThe Democratic resurgence was not restricted to Washington. The party also made major gains in gubernatorial elections, capturing Republican-held state executive offices in four states.A total of 36 states held gubernatorial elections, making the contests an important indicator of the political mood across the country. Democrats won 21 seats, flipping 4. Republicans won 12 seats.The biggest Democratic breakthroughs came in:Georgia: Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated her Republican opponent, delivering the governorship to Democrats for the first time in 24 years. She is the first woman and first Black person elected governor of Georgia.Ohio: Democrat Amy Acton defeated Trump-backed Vivek Ramaswamy, dealing a major blow to the president's preferred candidate in the home state of Vice-President JD Vance.Iowa: Democrat Rob Sand won the governorship, ending two decades of Republican control of the office.Texas: Democrat Gina Hinojosa pulled off one of the biggest upsets of the election, winning the governorship in a state Trump carried by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024.The Ohio result is particularly damaging for Trump. Ramaswamy, a prominent ally of the president and a former Republican presidential candidate, had received Trump's backing in the gubernatorial contest.His defeat suggests that the president's endorsement was insufficient to overcome the broader anti-Republican sentiment.The Texas result is arguably even more consequential. For Democrats, winning a statewide contest in a state that has remained a Republican stronghold in presidential politics is a major breakthrough.These victories also give Democrats greater influence over state-level policymaking, including education, healthcare, taxation, voting rules and the implementation of federal policies.8. Indian-American candidates The 2026 midterms have also been significant for the growing presence of Indian-American politicians in US electoral politics.Several Indian-American candidates have secured victories in congressional and state-level contests, while the defeat of Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio has provided one of the election's most closely watched reversals.Read also | Indian-American candidates shine in US midterms 2026: Who won from where? Full listDemocrat Pia Dandiya won Florida's 22nd Congressional District, defeating Republican Casey Askar. Election-night figures put her vote share at approximately 52% against Askar's 48%.Democratic Congressman Suhas Subramanyam secured re-election from Virginia's 10th Congressional District. He defeated Republican challenger Dave Beckwith, securing approximately 63.16% of the vote, or 173,106 ballots, against Beckwith's 34.66%, or 94,990 votes. Subramanyam, who became Virginia's first Indian-American member of Congress in 2024, will return for another term.Maryland Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller was re-elected alongside Democratic Governor Wes Moore, ensuring continuity in one of the most prominent state-level executive positions held by an Indian-American politician.Democratic lawmakers Ro Khanna, Ami Bera and Pramila Jayapal, also won their seats comfortably.9. Turbulent 2 years aheadPerhaps the most important consequence of the Democratic victory will be felt in Washington over the next two years.Trump entered his second term with Republicans controlling both chambers of Congress, giving him considerable freedom to pursue his legislative priorities.That political arrangement has now been flipped.With Democrats controlling the House and Senate, the president will face a far more formidable opposition.Congressional investigations, oversight hearings and subpoenas could become central features of the final two years of his presidency.Read also | 'I wasn't on ballot': Trump shrugs of midterm drubbing, shares photo of what's to comeDemocrats will have the authority to scrutinise federal agencies, examine the administration's handling of the Iran conflict, investigate spending and demand answers on issues ranging from immigration enforcement to tariffs and executive power.The Senate majority will also give Democrats greater influence over presidential appointments and the legislative process.However, congressional control does not automatically translate into the ability to reverse Trump's policies. The president retains executive powers and Trump has made it clear he will not take the defeat lying down.Read also|'They'll become garbage': Trump says he'll become 'Mr. Veto' if Democrats win midtermsAs Democrats celebrated their gains and took control of Congress, Trump responded with a pointed message on Truth Social. The US president posted an image of a red MAGA cap bearing the word 'VETO', in what appeared to be a defiant signal of how he intends to deal with a Democratic-controlled Congress.The message suggested that Trump was ready to use his presidential veto powers to block legislation pushed by Democrats, setting the stage for a potentially bitter legislative showdown between the White House and Capitol Hill.10. Implications for 2028The election also has major implications for the 2028 presidential race.For Republicans, the immediate challenge will be to explain the scale of the losses and decide whether to remain closely aligned with Trump or begin preparing for a political future beyond his presidency.For Democrats, the victory offers an opportunity to rebuild their national standing and develop a new generation of leaders.Hakeem Jeffries is likely to become one of the most powerful figures in Washington, while the party's successful candidates across the country could emerge as potential contenders for higher office.The election could also intensify the contest within the Democratic Party between its progressive wing and more centrist lawmakers over the direction of the party.The 2028 presidential election is still two years away, but the midterm results have dramatically changed the political landscape in which that contest will unfold.You use AI every day. articles.title: Michael Jordan donates $10 million to UNC in honour of his mother, setting a record for its School of Social Work as a global research centre takes her name and 10 students receive scholarships
articles.summary: Michael Jordan has made another major contribution to the University of North Carolina, this time directing a $10 million gift towards the university’s
articles.body: Michael Jordan has made another major contribution to the University of North Carolina, this time directing a $10 million gift towards the university’s School of Social Work in recognition of his mother, Deloris P. Jordan. Announced on October 5, 2026, the commitment is the largest single donation in the school's history. The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reported that it is intended to strengthen programmes supporting children, young people and families, while helping students facing the rising cost of postgraduate education. The money will also support research and community partnerships extending beyond North Carolina. For Jordan, a former UNC student who graduated in 1986, the donation carries a personal connection to his family's longstanding involvement in community welfare.Michael Jordan's $10 million donation puts his mother's name on a major UNC centreThe donation will support two existing initiatives at the university: the Jordan Institute for Families and the Global Social Development Innovations Center. The latter has been renamed the Deloris P. Jordan Global Social Development Innovations Center in recognition of the former basketball star's mother and her work supporting women, children and families.The university described the commitment as the largest individual contribution received by its School of Social Work. It is expected to strengthen the institution's research capacity and its work with organisations addressing social challenges at community level. The investment also gives the school additional resources to develop projects with partners outside the United States.UNC-Chapel Hill Chancellor Lee H. Roberts welcomed the contribution, saying it reflected Deloris Jordan's longstanding interest in improving conditions for children and families. He said the funding would help the school extend its work across North Carolina and internationally.Jordan also spoke about the personal significance of the decision. As reported by The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, he said, “My mother has always believed in the power of helping children, families and communities, and she has spent her life putting that belief into action.”“Honoring her through this gift to the UNC School of Social Work is truly meaningful to my family and to me. North Carolina will always be home, and I’m proud to support the social workers who are on the ground each and every day helping people navigate challenges, find opportunities and build stronger communities. I hope this gift helps make it possible for more students to pursue this important work.”10 students receive the first Jordan Family ScholarshipsPart of the $10 million commitment will go towards a new scholarship initiative called the Jordan Family Scholars programme. It is designed to help Master of Social Work students whose financial circumstances might otherwise make postgraduate study more difficult.The first ten recipients were introduced at the October 5 celebration at UNC. Each received a scholarship worth $12,500, providing direct financial assistance as they prepare for careers in social work. The university said, “We could not be more grateful to Michael Jordan for this generous investment in Carolina and the people and communities we serve.”The scholarships are also part of a wider effort to strengthen the social work workforce. Students trained at the school go on to work in settings where support can include family services, mental health, community development and assistance for vulnerable children.Deloris Jordan said, “I am deeply proud to have been part of the Carolina family for more than 40 years, and it is especially meaningful to know that this gift will strengthen the education and opportunities available to those preparing to serve others. Knowing that this work will extend beyond North Carolina through the Deloris P. Jordan Global Social Development Innovations Center makes it all the more special.”The Jordan family's connection with UNC dates back decadesThe new commitment builds on an association between the Jordan family and the university that extends well beyond Michael Jordan's time as a student. In 1996, he and his family established the Jordan Institute for Families, which works on issues affecting family stability and well-being.Its programmes cover a broad range of subjects, including maternal health, caregiving, mental health, home visiting and economic support. The institute also works to bring community experience into research, public policy and professional practice, with an emphasis on equity and engagement.The Global Social Development Innovations Center followed in 2017. Its work focuses on developing and assessing approaches intended to improve opportunities for young people and their families. Rather than relying solely on academic research, the centre works alongside local organisations and communities, drawing on their experience when designing and evaluating programmes.Deloris Jordan's work extends to women and children in KenyaBeyond her involvement with the university, Deloris Jordan has established projects addressing healthcare and support for vulnerable communities overseas. In 2010, she founded the Kenya Women and Children’s Wellness Centre in Nairobi, an organisation focused on providing healthcare to underserved populations.The centre works with survivors of gender-based violence and child abuse. Its activities also include training first responders to provide appropriate care, alongside community programmes and advocacy. According to UNC, the organisation has reached more than 203,700 people through its work.Her involvement in Kenya will feature during a global research symposium organised by the renamed centre alongside the donation celebration. Academics, practitioners and representatives from partner organisations in more than 20 countries are due to gather in Chapel Hill for the two-day event.The programme includes research presentations and panel discussions covering youth participation, emerging technology partnerships and approaches to sustainable development. A fireside conversation with Deloris Jordan will also examine her work in Kenya.A new investment in the university's social work missionMichael Jordan's latest gift adds to the family's existing involvement in programmes at UNC, but its scale makes it a significant development for the School of Social Work. The funding combines support for research and institutional initiatives with direct assistance for students preparing to enter the profession.For the university, the renamed centre and the Jordan Family Scholars programme create two distinct ways of carrying the family's contribution forward. One is focused on expanding research and partnerships across communities, while the other addresses the cost of education for future social workers. Jordan graduated from UNC in 1986 and has maintained a connection with the institution since his college years. His latest commitment places that relationship alongside his mother's work with families and communities, with the university set to direct the funding towards programmes operating both locally and internationally.You use AI every day. articles.title: Guernsey family may leave island over AI job concerns
articles.summary: A couple say they may leave Guernsey due to AI job concerns, after struggling to find work.
articles.body:
A couple says their family might leave Guernsey after claiming artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to them losing their jobs and left them struggling to find work.

Ania and Patryk Pawleta said they worked at the same tech company since 2018, and were both let go at the start of 2026. Patryk was a software developer and Ania was a product and image administrator.

Ania said she was made redundant "as part of wider redundancies" and was told by a manager that her duties would instead be done by AI.

Patryk said the company blamed his redundancy on "market changes" and he had to use AI "a lot towards the end" of his time at the firm. "AI is a reason why I am struggling to find another job," he said.

Ania said: "One of the reasons why I was let go with my company was AI."

"No-one is hiring because they only want AI to do the job. This is why we are looking for a job outside [the island]," Patryk added.

Patryk and Ania's former employer have been contacted for comment, but has not responded.

Since the start of the year, the Polish nationals, who have two children, have been relying on savings and sporadic income from Patryk's tech repair workshop to live on.

He said: "That workshop was 80% charity, 20% I was making some small amount of money. But, if I were to subtract the costs, I wasn't making anything."

He said social security had held back financial support due to the money he made from this workshop - although a case review is ongoing.

"I just did it from my heart and I suffer for it now," he said.

Director of operations for social security, States housing and inclusion Ed Ashton said: "To be eligible to receive unemployment benefit, a person must be available for work and actively seeking work."

He added: "Anything that might impact these requirements has to be investigated before a claim can be accepted."

On AI in the job market, Deputy Tom Rylatt, digital steering group representative for the Committee for Employment & Social Security, said: "AI and other emerging technologies are already beginning to reshape the labour market.

"Our job is to understand what these changes mean for Guernsey so that support services, retraining and skills interventions remain responsive to changing employment opportunities," he added.

Emily Gill, co-founder of skills company LEVRA and TEDx speaker, who has led talks in Guernsey on how the island should embrace AI, said: "There's a lot of fear around because people think 'could this tool you know wipe out whole swathes of jobs?'

"I think we're moving away from that slightly, and there's a realisation that a lot more value can be created using AI and there are going to be new types of jobs and new tasks that come from it."

articles.title: Fleabag star Phoebe Waller-Bridge offers London flat rent-free to new writers
articles.summary: Phoebe Waller-Bridge is donating the accommodation to playwrights from underprivileged backgrounds.
articles.body:
Fleabag creator, writer and actress Phoebe Waller-Bridge is offering a rent-free flat in London for writers early in their careers.

The 41-year-old has bought and donated the flat as part of a new theatre initiative Writers' Block, which aims to address the cost of London accommodation for playwrights from underprivileged backgrounds.

She bought the flat specifically for writers who are starting out and are struggling to afford accommodation in the capital, and has donated its use alongside what the scheme called a "generous financial contribution".

Her flat will be provided without rent, with the resident paying bills only.

Adolescence co-creator Jack Thorne – who wrote the films Wonder and Enola Holmes, as well as the Harry Potter And The Cursed Child stage play – is also providing financial backing to the scheme.

"I was lucky when I started out, my brother lived in Croydon and was able to put me up," he said.

"He did so, rather selflessly, for five years, before I moved to Luton and he got his peace.

"For many writers, the need for a roof makes writing impossible which is why this pilot is so important. If we want stories told about our complicated world, we need writers of every background writing them.

"If you're from privilege, your biggest problem is what to fill a page with. If you're not, so much of your struggle is about the need to survive."

Other backers include playwright and screenwriter James Graham, who wrote stage shows including Ink, Quiz and Dear England, as well as Happy Valley creator Sally Wainwright and The Crown's Peter Morgan.

Waller-Bridge's partner Martin McDonagh is also involved. He is best known for writing and directing films including Oscar and Bafta-winning The Banshees Of Inisherin and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.

Graham said the scheme tackled the class barrier facing writers and helped them avoid "giving up completely".

"The industry's urgent pursuit of representation is still letting down the biggest area of under-representation of all, which is class," he said.

"When I first made it to London, I slept on friends' floors and worked in call centres and bars while I wrote. Every spare room a scheme like this can give to writers starting out in London, not only helps them write but saves them from giving up completely."

Writers' Block was born from the Adopt a Playwright Award initiative, which was founded in 2008 and offers affordable accommodation to writers from disadvantaged backgrounds who need to be in the capital for meetings, rehearsals, performances and career opportunities.

Both schemes were created by Sofie Mason and Diana Jervis-Read.

articles.title: Fourth arrest after Halloween party stabbings in Chandler's Ford
articles.summary: All five boys who were injured had been invited to attend the supervised party on Saturday night.
articles.body:
A fourth boy has been arrested after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party in Hampshire.

Police were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to a home in Park Road in Chandler's Ford where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event over a garden fence.

One boy, 17, remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The other four boys, who all suffered serious injuries, have since been discharged.

A 16-year-old from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. Police have been given an extra 36 hours to question a 16 and 17-year-old, also from the city, who were held on Monday morning on suspicion of the same offence.

A 16-year-old boy from Bristol remains in custody having been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder on Monday night.

Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.

One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'.

"And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."

The other witness said: "A big group of people started shouting and then a fight broke out and then we just heard the dad tell everyone to leave.

"And that was when we saw someone injured on the floor."

Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.

The five boys who were stabbed had been invited to attend the supervised party.

Hampshire police said officers had carried out searches at three addresses linked to those arrested, two in Southampton and one in Bristol.

The force said several items had been seized, "forming part of our continued investigation".

It added since the investigation began, a number of witnesses had got in touch and officers had spoken to many of them.

Those who had already been in touch should wait to be contacted.

Anyone with information is still being urged to come forward.

The force said "no matter how small it may seem to you, it may be key to our inquiries".

Two churches in Chandler's Ford said earlier in the week they had opened their doors to offer support.

St Boniface in Hursley Road is open 09:00-17:00 through the week, while St Martin in the Wood in Queen's Road will open Wednesday from 15:00 to 17:00.

articles.title: Iran exempts Indian vessels from Hormuz curbs, citing medicine imports
articles.summary: Iran has exempted Indian vessels from restrictions on transit through the Strait of Hormuz, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday, as attacks on
articles.body: Iran has exempted Indian vessels from restrictions on transit through the Strait of Hormuz, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday, as attacks on shipping in the region continue to claim the lives of Indian seafarers. The latest exemption comes amid heightened concern over the safety of Indian nationals working aboard vessels in the Gulf, with the death toll from attacks on merchant shipping having risen to 23.Ahmad Hayat-Moghaddam, vice-chairman of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, said India, China, Iraq and Qatar had been granted exemptions and their vessels could pass through the strategic waterway without restrictions. Speaking at a meeting on economic and security conditions, he said Tehran had facilitated the passage of Indian ships to enable imports of medicines from India, while the arrangement with China was intended to secure Beijing’s political support.“We have already exempted four countries from restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz — India, China, Iraq and Qatar. They are free to pass through, and the Americans have no issues with them either,” Hayat-Moghaddam was quoted as saying by the Iranian Students’ News Agency.He said the exemption for Indian vessels was intended to facilitate medicine imports into Iran, while the arrangement for Chinese ships was aimed at securing Beijing’s political support. “We are doing business,” he said, adding that Tehran also collected money from Indian and Chinese vessels.The announcement comes against the backdrop of repeated attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which have killed Indian seafarers and prompted New Delhi to call for an end to attacks on commercial shipping. In the latest incident cited by Indian authorities, the Indian-flagged dhow MSV Al-Jusufi was struck by an unidentified aerial object near Oman’s coast. Thirteen crew members were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard, while one Indian sailor, Gandhar Nahim Ajij of Gujarat, died from his injuries.India condemned the attack and called for immediate de-escalation, urging all sides to restore free and unimpeded navigation through international waterways in accordance with international law. The Directorate General of Shipping had earlier advised ship owners and recruitment agencies against sending Indian nationals aboard vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, though the advisory was not binding. The Forward Seamen’s Union of India has said more than 4,000 Indian sailors remain aboard vessels in the region.Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts to prevent a renewed conflict are continuing. Iran’s military leadership has been urged to consider a Qatari-mediated proposal to halt the conflict. Qatari envoys reportedly travelled to Tehran to obtain Iran’s response to the proposed framework. However, the report said Iranian military strategists remain sceptical of a diplomatic settlement and view a return to confrontation with the US as the likelier scenario.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2009, Michael Jackson left a trust for his three children; 17 years later, daughter Paris is asking a court to move $600 million into it, while estate executors say unresolved tax litigation prevents full funding
articles.summary: Seventeen years after Michael Jackson’s death, his daughter Paris Jackson has returned to court with a blunt request: move $600 million from the late
articles.body: Seventeen years after Michael Jackson’s death, his daughter Paris Jackson has returned to court with a blunt request: move $600 million from the late singer’s estate into the family trust created for his three children. In a petition filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court, Paris argues that the Michael Jackson Family Trust remains unfunded despite the estate generating billions of dollars through music deals, property sales and other business ventures, reported LA Times. The estate’s executors have pushed back, saying they cannot fully fund the trusts until several legal matters are resolved, including a long-running dispute with the Internal Revenue Service. According to PEOPLE, the IRS initially sought about $700 million in taxes and penalties, although the estate says a ruling significantly reduced that amount. The matter has not been settled, and the estate argues it could still change.At the centre of the dispute is a familiar question in celebrity estates: when a fortune grows far beyond what anyone expected, how quickly should the beneficiaries receive what was promised to them? Paris says the answer is now. The estate says the answer must wait until the tax exposure and other legal risks are clearer. Read more details about this incident here, as per the reports.What Paris says was promisedMichael Jackson died in June 2009 at age 50, leaving behind three children: Prince, Paris and Bigi. Paris, now 28, says the trust was designed to give each child income from their share when they turned 21, followed by portions of the principal at 30 and additional distributions at 35 and 40.Her filing says that arrangement has not operated as intended. Prince is 29 and approaching 30, Paris turns 29 in April, and Bigi turns 25 in February. According to Paris, none of them has begun receiving the trust distributions contemplated by the estate plan, leaving them reliant on discretionary payments controlled by the estate’s remaining executor, John Branca. “More than seventeen years after his passing, Michael Jackson’s family trust remains unfunded,” the petition states, as quoted by PEOPLE. Paris also alleges that the executors said in 2011 that they would seek court approval to begin funding the trust, but that no such petition was ever filed.Why Paris wants $600 millionParis’s legal team argues that the estate has more than enough liquidity to make a substantial partial distribution. The petition points to the 2018 sale of the estate’s interest in EMI Music Publishing for $287.5 million, the $22 million sale of Neverland Ranch in 2020, and a major 2023 deal with Sony involving Michael’s music and other intellectual-property assets.Those transactions reportedly generated more than $1 billion in cash before taxes and expenses. Paris’s filing also cites an estate accounting showing approximately $850 million in cash and cash-equivalent assets as of December 2024. After accounting for potential liabilities, her lawyers conclude that roughly $600 million is available for distribution.The petition asks the court to order a preliminary transfer of $600 million to the Michael Jackson Family Trust, or another amount the judge considers appropriate. Paris argues that the estate’s executors have kept the beneficiaries dependent on them by controlling when and how much money is distributed.The estate’s responseThe estate denies that it has withheld money or reduced payments to the children. In a statement to PEOPLE, it called that allegation “a complete fabrication” and said more than $200 million had already been distributed for their benefit.It also pointed to the terms of Michael’s will, saying that none of his children receives a distribution until they are in their 30s. The estate said it looks forward to fully funding the children’s trusts once all issues are resolved, but insisted that outstanding legal matters must be addressed first.The IRS case is the largest unresolved issue. The estate says the tax dispute, which initially involved about $700 million in taxes and penalties, has been reduced by a court ruling but remains unsettled. Because the final liability could still change, the estate argues that moving hundreds of millions of dollars into the trust now would be premature.A wider family and estate conflictThe request is not happening in isolation. Paris has previously challenged aspects of the estate’s administration, and her latest petition alleges that her objections were met with public criticism, litigation and a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments to her and her brothers.Earlier this year, a Los Angeles judge ruled that $625,000 in bonus payments made by the estate’s executors to outside law firms in 2018 had to be returned to the estate. The ruling came after Paris objected to the payments. Attorneys for the estate disagreed with the decision but said they would comply with it.The estate was managed for years by Branca and John McClain, who were appointed co-executors after Michael’s death. McClain died in May 2026, leaving Branca as the remaining executor. That shift has added another layer of complexity to an estate already shaped by enormous commercial success and repeated legal disputes.What happens nextA judge is scheduled to hear Paris’s request on December 4. The hearing will not necessarily resolve the entire dispute, but it will determine whether the court believes a partial transfer to the family trust is justified before the estate’s outstanding legal matters are fully resolved.For the Jackson children, the case is about access to money their father intended to provide. For the estate, it is about protecting assets against a tax bill that could still move substantially. Both sides agree that Michael wanted his children provided for. They disagree sharply on whether the estate has honoured that intention, and on whether $600 million can safely be released now.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
